courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Who Was Socrates?
courses.description: Socrates is the quintessential philosopher--a man for all seasons, a foundational figure of the West.

source.text: PHIL 51. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-PAST or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Reason and Religion at the Dawn of Modern Science
courses.description: Students will read some of the most important philosophical reflections of the 17th and 18th centuries.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Theories in Human Nature
courses.description: Students will explore a variety of issues that arise when human beings begin to reflect on our own natures and will be introduced to main theories that have been developed. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Thinking about Time
courses.description: What is time? Do the past and the future exist, or only the present? Is the "flow of time" an objective feature of reality?

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Paradoxes
courses.description: Paradoxes have been a driving force in philosophy since the fourth century BCE. They force us to rethink old ideas and conceptions.

source.text: PHIL 55. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Abortion
courses.description: A general philosophical discussion of the value of life, the evil in death, and the wrongness of killing.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Race and Affirmative Action
courses.description: The goal of the course is to get a mature and correct understanding of race, racism, and affirmative action.

source.text: PHIL 57. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-POWER or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: From Vengeance to Mercy: Dealing with Evil
courses.description: This course will explore the ethical dimensions of the responses to evil that we have developed over history. Revenge, retribution, reparation; hatred, resentment, forgiveness; punishment, pardon, mercy.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Proofs of the Existence of God
courses.description: We will examine efforts in the history of philosophy to prove that God exists or that God does not exist. Our aim is to articulate and understand some of the underlying philosophical issues that are raised by these proofs and arguments. Honors version available.

source.text: PHIL 59. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Plato's Symposium and Its Influence on Western Art and Literature
courses.description: This seminar examines Plato's philosophical and literary masterpiece, The Symposium, and its influence on later artists and writers: we explore the Symposium itself, the ways in which the Symposium influenced later European artists and writers, and the importance of the Platonic view of love and beauty for modern artists and writers. Honors version available.

source.text: PHIL 60. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-AESTH or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First Year Seminar: The Self: Aspiration and Transformation
courses.description: Novels, memoirs, and aisles of self-help books attest to our desire to transform ourselves. Yet, the idea of self-transformation is puzzling. In this class, we will critically examine the idea of aspiration and transformation.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Philosophy with Children
courses.description: This seminar is designed to give students a unique, experiential perspective on philosophical inquiry by combining the philosophical study of ethics with virtual service in the community. We will examine philosophical questions about childhood and engage in philosophical interactions with children about a range of philosophical topics, with an emphasis on ethics and human values. Students perform 30 hours of service at a local K-5 school.

source.text: PHIL 62. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES, HI-SERVICE.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Mind, Brain, and Consciousness
courses.description: What are minds and how are they related to bodies?

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Philosophy through Mathematics
courses.description: This seminar introduces several of the central problems in philosophy through reflection on the nature of mathematics.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Ethics: Theoretical and Practical
courses.description: This seminar examines theoretical issues, relativism, utilitarianism, deontological ethics, and virtue ethics.

source.text: PHIL 66. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Issues in a World Society: Sports and Competition
courses.description: This seminar examines ethical issues in sports, including Title IX, gender equity, racism, sexism, cheating, violence, and drug use.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Moral Life
courses.description: This course will explore the meaning of basic moral concepts as they are understood in philosophy, science, and art. Honors version available.

source.text: PHIL 68. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Gateway to Philosophy, Politics, and Economics
courses.description: This course uses insights and techniques from philosophy, politics, and economics to answer questions like: What makes a modern civilization possible? How can our societies continue to improve? What role do property rights, markets, and political action play in creating flourishing civilizations? How do we address environmental degradation, distributive justice, and economic exploitation? Our answers will draw from rational choice theory, utility theory, game theory, public choice economics, etc. Course is limited to PPE minors.

source.text: PHIL 70. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-POWER or FC-VALUES, FC-LAB.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Evil
courses.description: What is evil? Who, if anyone, is responsible for it? How different are evil people from the rest of us? How should we respond to them? The course will explore the nature of evil through philosophy, nonfiction, fiction, and film.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Is Free Will an Illusion?
courses.description: This course will examine whether our belief in freedom of action is compatible with the modern picture of ourselves. Honors version available.

source.text: PHIL 76. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Moral Weakness and Conscience
courses.description: Is man's reason a powerful thing: if one had knowledge or belief about something that should be done, would that be enough to position one to do it?

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Death as a Problem for Philosophy: Metaphysical and Ethical
courses.description: This course explores both old and new questions regarding death. It will examine the presuppositions and cogency of the classical religious-philosophical conception of death.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Words That Bind: The Structure of Constitutions
courses.description: In this seminar we will examine a number of constitutions and try to determine what makes a constitution better or worse, and when it makes sense to borrow constitutional principles from other countries. We will also try our hand at designing a constitution.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Short Stories and Contemporary Social Problems
courses.description: We will read short stories and social science articles that address social problems such as child-rearing; social mobility; mass incarceration and race; the opiate crisis; tradition versus science. Students will explore the different ways in which literature, the humanities and the social sciences construct issues of social relevance, the opportunities and limits of these constructions, and what might be gained by using each to understand and respond to these issues.

source.text: PHIL 80. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Reason, Religion, and Reality in the Copernican Revolution
courses.description: The arguments by which Galileo and his contemporaries defended the Copernican model of the solar system puzzle philosophers even today. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Persons and Identity
courses.description: An introduction to the topic of personal identity, focused on epistemological, ethical, and metaphysical themes. The course examines what personal identity over time consists in, whether and how we can know such identity, under what conditions our personal identity is liable to change, and what this implies for our values and projects.

source.text: PHIL 86. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: First Year Seminar: Special Topics
courses.description: Special Topics Course. Content will vary each semester.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy: Central Problems, Great Minds, Big Ideas
courses.description: An introduction to philosophy focusing on a few central problems, for example: free will, the basis of morality, the nature and limits of knowledge, and the existence of God. Honors version available.
courses.gen_ed_raw: FY-LAUNCH (only designated sections), FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

source.text: PHIL 101. | 3 Credits. | FY-LAUNCH (only designated sections), FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy: Central Problems, Great Minds, Big Ideas
courses.description: This course introduces students to the experience of thinking like philosophers and aims at developing students' capacity to think carefully and critically about philosophical arguments. The central skills to be practiced are those involved in productive philosophical discussion. The course emphasizes how philosophy is and has been done through dialogue, that philosophical claims must be tested against the objections of one's fellow thinkers, and how philosophical disagreement can lead to productive insights.

source.text: PHIL 102. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES, COMMBEYOND.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: How to Reason and Argue: An Introduction to Critical Thinking
courses.description: A course on how to identify, analyze, and evaluate arguments by other people and how to construct arguments. Topics include argument reconstruction, informal logic, fallacies, introductory formal logic, probabilistic reasoning.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophical Texts that Changed the World: An Introduction to Philosophy through Great Works
courses.description: An introduction to philosophy focusing on several great books from the history of Western philosophy. See course description at the department's website for which books will be covered each semester. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 110 and PHIL 113 . Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosopher Queens: World Philosophies through Women's Texts
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to world philosophies through close readings of philosophical texts attributed to or written by women in different time-periods from across the globe. We will practice the art of reading, understanding, and philosophically engaging with great historical works of philosophy while also examining the political inequalities, social structures, and contemporary practices from within which these women philosophers wrote and were trying to make their voices heard.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Making Sense of Ourselves
courses.description: An examination of some of the most influential attempts to understand human beings, their lives, and their moral and political values. Authors may include Plato, Aristotle, and Nietzsche. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophical Texts that Changed the World: An Introduction To Philosophy Through Great Works
courses.description: An introduction to philosophy focusing on several great books from the history of Western philosophy. See course description at the department's website for which books will be covered each semester. Special emphasis on practicing, engaging in, and discussing the activity of oral communication and communal deliberation. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 113 and PHIL 110 .

source.text: PHIL 113. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-VALUES, COMMBEYOND.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Reason, Faith, and God: Philosophy of Western Religion
courses.description: A philosophical inquiry into the problems of religious experience and belief, as expressed in philosophic, religious, and literary documents from traditional and contemporary sources. Honors version available.

source.text: PHIL 134. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES. | RELI 126 .

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Knowledge and Society
courses.description: An examination of questions about knowledge, evidence, and rational belief as they arise in areas of social life such as democratic politics, the law, science, religion, and education. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: AI and the Future of Humanity: Philosophical Issues about Technology and Human Survival
courses.description: This course investigates philosophical issues arising from advanced forms of technology, in particular artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and biological augmentation. We will consider questions about the dangers and benefits of AI, survival in non-biological ways, moral constraints on AI, the relationship between human and machine morality, and others. Honors version available.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethics of Emerging Technology
courses.description: Technology is reshaping our experiences in ways that, until recently, seemed like something out of science fiction: we now live in a world with generative AI assistants, self-driving cars, biometric authenticators, deepfakes, and DNA tests. How should we evaluate the impact these technologies have had and will have on our lives? In this course, we will apply methods of philosophical inquiry to carefully think through some of the moral questions raised by new technologies and provide a more nuanced evaluation of its impact on human activity.

source.text: PHIL 144. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES, COMMBEYOND.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Language, Communication, and Human and Animal Minds
courses.description: An examination of the differences between natural human languages and other communication systems. Includes a philosophical inquiry into how languages relate to the world and the mind. Honors version available.

source.text: PHIL 145. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-POWER. | LING 145 .

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Theory, Evidence, and Understanding in Science
courses.description: What is distinctive about the kind of knowledge called "science"? What is scientific explanation? How are scientific theories related to empirical evidence? Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 150 and PHIL 151 . Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Theory, Evidence, and Understanding in Science (CommBeyond)
courses.description: What is distinctive about the kind of knowledge called ''science''? What is scientific explanation? How are scientific theories related to empirical evidence? An examination of these and related issues with special focus on developing oral communication skills. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 151 and PHIL 150 .

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of the Social Sciences
courses.description: How do social sciences explain human actions? Are there social facts over and above facts about various individuals? Do values enter into social science?
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Truth and Proof: Introduction to Mathematical Logic
courses.description: Introduces the theory of deductive reasoning, using a symbolic language to represent and evaluate patterns of reasoning. Covers sentential logic and first-order predicate logic. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Logic and Decision Theory
courses.description: A broader discussion of practical reasoning, including inductive and deductive logic, which provides a good introduction to decision and game theory that is important for the social sciences, especially economics. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Virtue, Value, and Happiness: An Introduction to Moral Theory
courses.description: Exploration of different philosophical perspectives about right and wrong, personal character, justice, moral reasoning, and moral conflicts. Readings drawn from classic or contemporary sources. Critical discussion emphasized. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 160 and PHIL 161 . Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Virtue, Value, and Happiness: An Introduction to Moral Theory
courses.description: Exploration of different philosophical perspectives about right and wrong, personal character, justice, moral reasoning, and moral conflicts. Readings drawn from classic or contemporary sources. Special emphasis on practicing, engaging in, and discussing the activity of oral communication and communal deliberation. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 160 and PHIL 161 .

source.text: PHIL 161. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES, COMMBEYOND.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Practical Ethics: Moral Reasoning and How We Live
courses.description: Topics may include war, medical ethics, media ethics, sexual ethics, business ethics, racism, sexism, capital punishment, and the environment. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Morality and Business
courses.description: An examination of business ethics and the types of ethical dilemmas people may face in business practices.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Bioethics
courses.description: An examination of ethical issues in the life sciences and technologies, medicine, public health, and/or human interaction with nonhuman animals or the living environment. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Liberty, Rights, and Responsibilities: Introduction to Social Ethics and Political Thought
courses.description: An examination of major issues in political philosophy, e.g., liberty, individual rights, social responsibility, legal authority, civil authority, civil disobedience. Readings include classical and contemporary writings. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Free Speech and the Norms of Public Discourse
courses.description: An investigation of the nature, value, and limits of free speech and viewpoint diversity, and of the norms we should adhere to when engaging in political discourse with one another. Uses the tools and methods of philosophical thought. Special attention to these questions in the setting of a contemporary university.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophical Foundations of American Democracy
courses.description: This course explores the political philosophies that shaped the United States, such as the Enlightenment, classical republicanism (liberty, self-government, rule of law), and constitutionalism. By reading and discussing a variety of philosophical and historical texts, students will learn how these ideas formed the foundation of American democracy and how later generations continued the effort to form "a more perfect union".

source.text: PHIL 175. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-VALUES, FAD.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Humor
courses.description: A course on philosophical issues related to laughter and humor. Historical and contemporary philosophical theories of humor; connections between traditional issues in aesthetics and humor; moral questions about humor, such as what is involved in a joke being racist/sexist/homophobic; and connections between jokes and various epistemological fallacies.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Aesthetics and the Philosophy of Art
courses.description: The nature of art and artworks and their aesthetic appraisal. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Special Topics in Philosophy, FC-VALUES
courses.description: Intensive exploration and discussion of selected topics in philosophy.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Wonder, Myth, and Reason: Introduction to Ancient Greek Science and Philosophy
courses.description: The emergence of philosophy in Greece during the sixth century BCE and its development during the classical period. The major figures studied are the Pre-Socratic philosophers, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Perspectives on Gender, Race, and Marginality in Ancient Greek Philosophy, Science, and Medicine
courses.description: This course studies through the examination of several infamous, ignored, or otherwise uncharted Ancient Greek texts the views about gender and race as presented in ancient Greek philosophy, medicine, and science. Our aims are to generate a new understanding of how the male elite used such views to further promote or justify (or perhaps challenge) the existing marginalization and silencing of women, foreigners, and less privileged men.

source.text: PHIL 211. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER, RESEARCH.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Asian Philosophy
courses.description: An examination of some of the philosophical traditions of Asia. Possible topics include Advaita Vedanta, Nyaya-Vaisheshika, Madhyamaka Buddhism, neo-Confucianism, Mohism, and philosophical Taoism.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Medieval Philosophy
courses.description: A survey of medieval philosophy from Augustine through Ockham. Topics: God and the world, faith and reason, knowledge and reality, the problem of universals. Additional main authors: Anselm, Aquinas, Duns Scotus.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: 17th and 18th Century Western Philosophy
courses.description: A study of some major philosophical works from this period, including works by authors such as Descartes, Spinoza, Locke, Berkeley, Leibniz, Hume, and/or Kant. Honors version available.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Existential Philosophy and the Meaning(lessness) of Life
courses.description: A survey of European philosophers in the phenomenological and existentialist traditions. Philosophers studied may include Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre, Camus. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: American Philosophy
courses.description: An exploration of the distinctively American approaches to philosophy from Jonathan Edwards to the present.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: 20th-Century Western Philosophy
courses.description: An introductory survey of British and Continental philosophy in the 20th century.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Mind, Matter, and Metaphysics: the Philosophy of Experience and Reality
courses.description: Topics in metaphysics and/or epistemology, such as: Is your mind different from your brain? Is it possible for us to know anything about the external world? Do we have free will? What distinguishes reasonable from unreasonable belief? Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Inductive Logic and the Scientific Method
courses.description: This course examines the role that inductive logic plays in scientific reasoning. Questions to be considered include: Are scientific theories distinguished from pseudoscience by being testable against our observations? Can we prove our best scientific theories to be true? Are we justified in making predictions about the future on the basis of past observations? The course examines these and other questions about confirming scientific theories by using the apparatus provided by the probability calculus.

source.text: PHIL 251. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-QUANT, RESEARCH.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethics in Action
courses.description: Ethics Bowl provides a unique experiential opportunity for students to apply theory to practical global issues. Students will prepare cases to present locally and at Ethics Bowl competition. Permission of the instructor.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit. 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethics, Politics, and Technology
courses.description: In the near future, our taxis will be driver-less, our wars will be fought by autonomous drones, and our towns will be kept safe by algorithms foreseeing crimes. This course explores the ethical implications of this new technological revolution and invites students to debate the challenges it engenders. We will debate how new technologies ought to be governed and what limits should be imposed on their implementation.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Not All Fun and Games: Ethics of Sports
courses.description: An analysis of the moral significance of sports, the nature of sport and competition, and issues such as racism, gender equity, violence, and performance-enhancing drugs.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: The Ethics of Peace, War, and Defense
courses.description: An analysis of ethical issues that arise in peace, war, and defense, e.g., the legitimacy of states, just war theory, terrorism, weapons of mass destruction.

source.text: PHIL 272. | 3 Credits. | FC-POWER or FC-VALUES. | POLI 272 , PWAD 272 .

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Justice, Rights, and the Common Good: Philosophical Perspectives on Social and Economic Issues
courses.description: This course will focus on justice and the common good, applying theoretical justifications to contemporary social and economic issues. Readings will include classical and contemporary literature on the nature of justice and rights. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Race, Racism, and Social Justice: African-American Political Philosophy
courses.description: Race, identity, discrimination, multiculturalism, affirmative action, and slave reparations in the writings of Walker, Delany, Douglass, Cooper, DuBois, King, and Malcolm X. Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Moral and Philosophical Issues of Gender in Society
courses.description: A survey of feminist perspectives on topics such as the meaning of oppression, sexism and racism, sex roles and stereotypes, ideals of female beauty, women in the workplace, pornography, rape. Honors version available.

source.text: PHIL 275. | 3 Credits. | FC-POWER or FC-VALUES. | WGST 275 .

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ideology, Capitalism, and Critique
courses.description: This course studies how (oftentimes implicit) ideological commitments shape our culture and our social reality. We will explore the Marxist tradition and the Frankfurt School Critical Theory, as well as contemporary applications and critiques of ideology in thinkers such as Jaeggi, Fraser, Shelby, and Haslanger.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Latin American Philosophy
courses.description: This class addresses perennial philosophical questions about existence, morality, knowledge, and meaning through texts and authors from Latin America. The clash of conquistadors with pre-Columbian peoples, the wars of independence, and the unique mestizo heritage of Latin America provide a rich context to frame traditional philosophical questions in a new light.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Morality, Law, and Justice: Issues in Legal Philosophy
courses.description: Explores issues in legal philosophy such as, What is law? Does it serve justice or undermine it? Can punishment be justified? When is a person responsible? Honors version available.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Human Rights: Philosophical Interrogations
courses.description: The philosophy of human rights addresses questions about the existence, content, nature, universality, justification, and legal status of human rights. The strong claims made on behalf of human rights frequently provoke skeptical doubts and countering philosophical defenses. These will be addressed through classical and contemporary history of philosophy.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Moral and Philosophical Issues in Education
courses.description: A critical examination of the moral and philosophical issues in education: What does it mean to be well educated? What is a liberal education? Honors version available.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Field Work in Philosophy: Introducing Philosophy in Primary and Secondary Schools
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. This course combines on-campus structured learning with substantial on-site field work incorporating philosophy into the primary and/or secondary school curriculum. Philosophy subjects and school partners will vary by semester.

source.text: PHIL 292. | 3 Credits. | Prerequisite, two previous PHIL courses. | FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy across the Lifespan
courses.description: This is a high-impact service-learning course that aims to promote experiential learning in philosophy by combining traditional elements of classroom study with service in the community (HI-SERVICE). Students will have the unique opportunity to teach and learn philosophy alongside older adults in the Triangle area, thereby integrating the academic study of philosophy with community engagement.

source.text: PHIL 294. | 3 Credits. | Prerequisite, One prior Philosophy course required. | FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES, HI-SERVICE.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Reasoning Together: Philosophy through Dialogue and Podcast
courses.description: What does it take to speak and listen philosophically? How do we think and inquire together? This course is a hands-on exploration of how to link out loud through an engagement with one of the most popular philosophical mediums: podcasts. Students will reflect on and engage in meaningful, rigorous, and respectful philosophical conversation, even when the topic is abstract, personal, or controversial.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Special Topics in Philosophy, FC-KNOWING
courses.description: Intensive exploration and discussion of selected topics in philosophy.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy as a Way of Life: Spiritual Exercise across the Globe
courses.description: What does it mean to live philosophically? This course presents philosophy not only as an intellectual discipline, but also as a way of life and as a global, transformative practice. Students explore how classical and pre-modern traditions from around the world championed diverse forms of spiritual and ethical self-cultivation.

source.text: PHIL 310. | 3 Credits. | Prerequisite, One previous PHIL course. | FC-PAST, COMMBEYOND.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Metaphysics
courses.description: An examination of general theories of the nature of reality. What kinds of things exist? What are space, time, and causation? Are abstract entities (such as numbers) real?
requisites_notes: could not interpret: 'Prerequisite, one previous PHIL course' (unrecognized text: 'one previous PHIL course')

source.text: PHIL 330. | 3 Credits. | Prerequisite, one previous PHIL course. | FC-KNOWING.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Theory of Knowledge
courses.description: What is knowledge and how does it relate to belief, justification, and truth? What makes beliefs reasonable or irrational? Can skepticism be defeated?
requisites_notes: could not interpret: 'Prerequisite, one previous PHIL course' (unrecognized text: 'one previous PHIL course')

source.text: PHIL 335. | 3 Credits. | Prerequisite, one previous PHIL course. | FC-KNOWING.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Mind
